Your Why Us draft says the college has a world-class faculty and a vibrant community. Where did you read that?
On their website, more or less. It is how they describe themselves.
Exactly. So when you send it back to them, what have you told them that they did not already know?
Nothing, I suppose. It is their sentence with my name on it.
Try this instead. Find one course, one person and one thing you could only do there, and check that each one is real.
There is a course on the chemistry of pigments that is taught jointly by an art historian and a chemist.
Now that is interdisciplinary in a way you can prove. What does it have to do with you?
Since the Vermeer lesson I have wanted to know why that blue was so expensive, and what it is actually made of.
When I was a counselor in my first year, I let a student send a supplement that named the wrong professor. Nobody has forgotten it, least of all me.

Okay, everyone, if you can gather around the steps for a second. I have given this tour about sixty times, and I can tell you exactly what families ask about. Dorms, food, and whether the gym is open late. Those are fair questions, and I am happy to answer them. But I wish more of you asked what a normal Tuesday in class actually feels like, because that is what you will be doing for four years. Mine looked like this. My first-year seminar had twelve students around one table, and every single week there was an object from the campus collection in the middle of it. A coin, a letter, a small painting. We were not allowed to look anything up until we had spent twenty minutes just describing it. So here is my advice for your Why Us supplement, and I promise it is not in the brochure. Write about something you saw or did on this visit that you could not have read on our website. The admissions office knows what the website says. They wrote it.

Thank you all for coming. Let me tell you what I do not care about when I meet students who are thinking about art history. I do not care whether you already know the names of famous artists, or whether you can list the movements of the twentieth century in order. You will learn those things here, quickly, and frankly they are the easy part. What I look for is harder to fake. I look for students who ask a real question about an object, and who are willing to stay with that question long enough to discover that their first answer was wrong. That willingness is rare, and it is the foundation of everything we do. One more thing, since some of you are writing supplements. Please be careful with the word passion. Everyone uses it, so it tells me nothing at all. I would much rather hear about one object that kept you awake at night, and what you still do not understand about it.
